lai.ai-you-can-use.l01.question: What makes a suggestion worth using?

sections.title: Start with what success needs
sections.text: For the fictional club, success means six students can join an activity within 10 minutes, with no spending and no phones. Those are constraints: conditions the result must satisfy. An exciting description does not make a plan fit.

sections.title: Inspect the draft, one condition at a time
sections.text: The proposed online tournament takes 45 minutes, costs money and needs phones. It fails all three checks. You do not need an AI tool to notice this. Put the brief beside the suggestion and mark each mismatch.

sections.title: Repair it, then check what you missed
sections.text: A possible repair uses one minute to explain a scrap-paper word game, seven minutes to play and two minutes to share. That totals 10 minutes and needs no spending or phones. It is still a proposal: ask the club organizer whether everyone can read, write or contribute another way.

practice.title: Start with your own plan
instructions: Write a first plan before opening the worked example. Include setup, activity and clearing away in 10 minutes.
Check no spending and no phones. Choose a tool or explain why none is needed.
Keep this first version for comparison; you will adapt it to a changed constraint later.
practice.selfCheck: Is every constraint visible in your plan? What still needs checking with the club organizer?

lai.ai-you-can-use.l01.takeaway: Define useful → check every constraint → revise or reject → explain your decision.
lai.ai-you-can-use.l01.independentPractice: Tomorrow, try the same three-constraint check on a fictional plan without reopening the worked example. Explain one reason to use a tool and one reason not to.

lai.ai-you-can-use.l02.question: Is it following a rule, learning a pattern, or making something?

sections.title: Three approaches that still work together
sections.text: A rule-based tool follows a condition a person wrote: if the timer reaches zero, show a reminder. A learned classifier fits patterns from examples, such as labeled plant photos. A generator produces content, such as a new announcement. These are overlapping descriptions, not a timeline where each new approach erases the last.

sections.title: Training changes; inference uses
sections.text: During training, a model is adjusted using data. When a trained plant model labels a new photo, it is doing inference. That one prediction does not prove the label is correct or mean the model learned from the photo. A product may separately collect data for later training; do not assume it does or does not.

sections.title: Test beyond the examples it learned from
sections.text: Imagine a fictional leaf classifier trained only on clear daylight photos. A useful test includes different photos with independently checked labels, including shade or unfamiliar backgrounds. Record which predictions match and which fail. Testing only the training examples can hide a model that learned those examples but performs poorly on new ones.

practice.title: Your turn: design two tools
instructions: On paper or in your own words, invent a rule with an explicit if/then condition. You do not need to code it.
Invent a learned tool. Name the examples it would train on and the prediction it would make.
Inspect the prediction table and save your error analysis. Then design two new test cases for your own learned tool, with expected answers and a way to check them.
Save your designs and test plan in the final step. Use fictional objects or made-up club tasks; do not upload photos or personal data.
practice.selfCheck: Can you explain why your test examples are separate from training? What would you do if the tool fails one?

lai.ai-you-can-use.l02.takeaway: Ask how it works, where its examples came from, and how you would check a new result.
lai.ai-you-can-use.l02.independentPractice: Without the notes, explain a timer, a learned classifier and a generator to someone—or write the explanation yourself. Include how their functions can overlap.

Actual means the independently checked label; Model means its prediction. Compare the two and separate new test examples from reused training examples.
